Donn Jones By Nikki Ross – Reporter, Nashville Business Journal Sep 29, 2026 JavaScript is disabled To continue reading this content, please enable JavaScript in your browser settings and refresh this page. Listen to this article 3 min Story Highlights What's This? Saravir Biopharma licensed Vanderbilt Health's measles antibodies for clinical development. The United States reported 3,659 confirmed measles cases across 47 states. The antibody treatment targets pregnant women, infants and immunocompromised people. One of Vanderbilt Health’s antibodies has been picked up by a California company for the next stage of development amid a rapid rise in cases nationwide. Saravir Biopharma Inc. has licensed the health system’s antibodies that could potentially neutralize the measles virus, and is now looking for funding for further development and clinical testing, according to the health system. If the company can obtain the funding, it could have the first monoclonal antibody therapy for the highly infectious respiratory virus in 18 months to two years. “We fast-tracked this research to discover human antibodies for measles virus because of the emerging outbreaks of infections,” said Dr. James Crowe Jr., director of the Vanderbilt Center for Antibody Therapeutics, in a press release. As of Sept. 24, there were 3,659 confirmed measles cases this year, 95% of which are from outbreaks, in the United States across 47 states, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the most cases reported since 1990. So far this year, there have been 40 new outbreaks of measles. In 2025 there were 48 total outbreaks, up 200% from the 16 outbreaks reported in 2024. The uptick in outbreaks is from a decline in vaccination rates, according to Vanderbilt Health. Last month, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported two measles-associated deaths in unvaccinated people, the first such fatalities in 35 years. Since then, two more deaths have been reported by the state. “This could skyrocket into a huge problem,” said Dr. Ron Moss, Saravir Biopharma president and CEO, in the release. The antibody treatment is meant for those who cannot safely receive the vaccine, according to Vanderbilt Health. This includes pregnant women, infants under 12 months of age and immunocompromised people. Moss said these people are the focus of Saravir Biopharma’s anti-measles antibody development program. “Two years [to the clinic] is a conservative estimate,” Moss said in the release. “When we get the funding, we think that timeline could be expedited considerably.” Vanderbilt’s Vaccine Center, also run by Crowe and made up of a team of roughly 50 researchers, has had seven antibodies turned into vaccines for people, including Covid-19, Rift Valley Fever virus, Marburg virus, Enterovirus D68 and Chikungunya. content: Skip to Article Set weather Back To Main Menu Close Weather in - Change Location Current -Mostly Sunny TonightLow -Mostly Sunny TomorrowHigh -Mostly Sunny Full Weather Report Unlimited Digital Access - $1 for the first month - Sale ends 10/4/26 News Pennsylvania just hit a measles milestone that has health officials deeply concerned Updated: Oct. 02, 2026, 11:36 a.m. |Published: Oct. 02, 2026, 11:26 a.m. Health officials in Pennsylvania are working to contain a measles outbreak that has reached 943 cases across 39 counties after reporting a fifth measles-associated death. (AP Photo/Mary Conlon, File)AP Photo/Mary Conlon Set as Google Preferred Source By Chris Pugh, cleveland.com Pennsylvania health officials say a fifth person linked to the state’s measles outbreak has died, marking another troubling development in the largest active measles outbreak in the United States. The person lived in Lancaster County, was not vaccinated and tested positive for measles, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Health. The state now has 943 confirmed measles cases spread across 39 counties. Health officials reported 40 new cases since earlier in the week. Pennsylvania has become the center of the nation’s biggest ongoing measles outbreak as public health workers continue efforts to slow the spread of the virus, WHYY reported. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases in the world. It spreads through coughing, sneezing and close contact. Fox 29 reported. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person leaves an area. Symptoms often begin with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes before a rash develops, PennWatch said. Officials say nearly all of Pennsylvania’s cases have been among people who were not vaccinated. Only four cases have involved vaccinated individuals. More than 176 people have required hospitalization during the outbreak. Health experts say vaccination remains the best protection against measles. Pennsylvania has increased vaccination efforts by offering clinics throughout affected communities. State officials say the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is highly effective and remains the strongest tool for preventing serious illness and death. content_title: Measles cases top 900 in PA
content: An electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia S. Goldsmith; William Bellini, Ph.D./Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS/TNS) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: September 29, 2026 at 10:15 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The number of reported measles cases in Pennsylvania has topped 900. The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported in its latest update Monday that 903 measles cases have been confirmed across 39 counties. Berks County remains at five reported cases, according to the department’s dashboard, pa.gov/measles . The department’s update noted the following: New positive cases since Sept. 25: 13 • Total counties: 39 • Total cumulative cases: 903 • Total hospitalizations: 176 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 4 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the dashboard, Lancaster County remains the leader in cases with 363. Cases in the region: Chester County, 83; Lebanon County, 21; Montgomery County, 3; Lehigh County, 2; and Schuylkill County, 1. State health officials said they have administered more than 5,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 173 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since late April when the outbreak began. Overall, state health center staff have administered more than 7,900 MMR vaccine doses this year. In a typical month, state health care providers administer about 25,000 doses of the MMR vaccine. In August, more than 49,000 MMR vaccines were given statewide and more than 38,000 doses have been administered over the first three weeks of September, officials said. The department continues to advise that the best protection against measles is to get fully vaccinated. The two-dose MMR vaccine boosts a person’s immune system and provides 97% lifetime protection. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a health care provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your health care provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). content_title: Ohio measles cases spread to 4 more counties in latest ODH update
content: News Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles cases spread to 4 more counties in latest ODH update Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Oct. 2, 2026, 10:21 a.m. ET Ohio's 2026 measles outbreak has spread to four new counties, bringing the state's total to 206 cases this year. The vast majority of measles cases in Ohio are among individuals who have not been vaccinated. Health officials state the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best way to protect against the disease. Measles has spread to four new counties as Ohio's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state had 10 new cases in the past week, a 37.5% decrease from the 16 new cases the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 206 cases in 20 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Oct. 1. Total cases in Ohio this year have increased in recent weeks: 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Ashland, Stark, Vinton and Wood counties all join the list this week, each with one reported case. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Sept. 25 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 3,782 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio; counties reporting cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 1 (one new case) Ashtabula: 32 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 7 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 49 (five new cases) Harrison: 11 Holmes: 9 Knox: 5 Meigs: 4 Morgan: 3 Morrow: 9 (one new case) Ottawa: 1 Portage: 1 Stark: 1 (one new case) Trumbull: 8 Tuscarawas: 13 Vinton: 1 (one new case) Wayne: 44 Wood: 1 (one new case) The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least four people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 23, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Where are measles cases spreading in Ohio? Portage County confirmed its first measles case, the county Health District announced Sept. 8. At the time, no public exposure locations associated with this case had been identified. Harrison County Public Health reported one case of measles as of Aug. 7, but the state dashboard shows additional cases there. Geauga Public Health reports that the individuals with measles visited several locations while able to spread the virus, including Bloomfield Horse Sale, 2211 Kinsman Road NW, on July 18. The Tuscarawas health department reports that another of its cases was exposed at the Bloomfield Livestock Auction, at the same address as Bloomfield Horse Sale, on on the same day. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination for measles has declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023, the most recent year available from ODH. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before, through four days after, a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. content: Open menu NTD Television U.S.ChinaWorldPoliticsHealthBusinessEntertainmentSports More ●LIVE search EN▼ NTD Television NewsUS NewsState News Indiana Warns of Measles Exposure at the Zoo Indiana authorities said a total of 24 Measles cases have been reported statewide so far this year, including six in Wayne and six in Switzerland. By Juliette Fairley | Published: 10/2/2026, 12:32:17 PM EDT This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) When an individual infected with measles visited the Fort Wayne Zoo last weekend, Indiana health authorities believe other people at the zoo may have been exposed to the virus. Also known as rubeola, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes measles on its website as being a highly contagious viral respiratory illness. The exposure began at the Fort Wayne Zoo on Sept. 27 at approximately 11:30 a.m. and ended at 5 p.m., according to the Allen County Department of Health. The venue is formerly known as the Fort Wayne Children's Zoo and is a popular regional attraction. “As vaccination rates wane and measles continues to circulate in Indiana and across the U.S., exposure to the virus will become more likely,” officials said in a statement online. A total of 24 Measles cases have been reported statewide so far this year, including six in Wayne and six in Switzerland, according to an Indiana Department of Health (IDOH) surveillance tracker. Other cases occurred in Adams, Allen, DeKalb, LaGrange, Ohio, Parke, and Randolph. As of Sept. 26, six of the measles cases required hospitalization. The virus spreads through the air by coughing and sneezing and can linger long after an infected person leaves. As a result, visitors who were at the zoo during the identified time frame are urged to check their measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) immunization record and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. “We are thankful for the Allen County Department of Health for their attentiveness and expertise,” Fort Wayne Zoo executive director and CEO Rick Schuiteman said. “The safety of our guests, staff and volunteers is incredibly important and we will continue to follow the lead of the Allen County Department of Health.” Measles symptoms include a fever of 101 degrees or higher, sore throat, small white spots inside cheeks, red, watery eyes, coughing, runny nose, and a rash that starts on the face and spreads across the body. For those who are unvaccinated and believe they were exposed at the zoo, the health department recommends self-quarantining for three weeks and consulting with physicians. The IDOH surveillance tracker further shows that nine Measles cases occurred in individuals between the ages of 5 and 24 years old, eight cases occurred in individuals between the ages of 25 and 49 years old, and 3 cases occurred among individuals between the ages of 50 and 64 years old. “We urge anyone with questions or concerns to reach out to their local health department or a medical professional,” Schuiteman added

content: Skip to main content Local News Five more measles cases confirmed in Georgia WUGA | By Maura Potvin Published October 1, 2026 at 3:40 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Your browser doesn’t support HTML5 audio Fictional Blood samples with infected measles virus, with stethoscope, mask and syringe and other stuff. MAURO RODRIGUES/Mauro Rodrigues - stock.adobe.com The Georgia Department of Public Health has confirmed five additional measles cases in Georgia. The cases were among siblings in a Jasper County family. The Georgia Department of Public Health said the siblings were either unvaccinated or had not completed two full doses of the MMR vaccine. These five additional cases bring the total number of confirmed measles cases in Georgia to 21 in 2026. There were 10 confirmed cases in Georgia in 2025. Measles symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a rash of tiny red dots. The health department recommends anyone experiencing these symptoms should call their healthcare provider immediately. According to the health department, over 95% of people who receive one dose of the MMR vaccine develop immunity to all three of the viruses. A second dose of the vaccine boosts immunity to 98%. The Jasper County cases are not related to the outbreak out of a Cobb County daycare. (AFP) Short Url https://arab.news/6v7gz 1 in 1,000 infected children may develop a condition leading to brain damage Most face immune amnesia and secondary infections Updated 27 September 2026 18:06 SHEHAB SUMON September 27, 2026 18:03 DHAKA: The youngest generation of Bangladeshis could face lasting developmental complications from measles, doctors have warned, as the country battles an outbreak that has already killed more than 1,000 children. The outbreak was officially declared on March 15, when the Directorate General of Health Services began to publish daily infection figures. At least 186,813 suspected cases and 1,087 deaths have been reported since, with most infections occurring in children below two years of age. “I have never in my life seen measles in a three-month-old infant, but I saw it this time,” Dr. ASM Mahmuduzzaman, pediatrics professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College and Hospital in Dhaka, told Arab News. “There is a concern that these children who had measles may face long-term complications.” He estimated that while the official number of recorded confirmed and suspected infections was nearly 200,000, the actual figure could even be as high as 500,000. One of the most dangerous measles complications is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a chronic, neurodegenerative illness caused by the persistence of the measles virus in the brain. The symptoms only become apparent after a few years. “Suddenly, with or without fever, they will experience convulsions. If this doesn’t fall into the hands of a specialist or an experienced doctor, the underlying cause of these convulsions will remain unidentified,” Mahmuduzzaman said. “The manifestations will be like myoclonic jerks. It could involve involuntary movements in a hand, a leg, or a specific muscle group, leading to convulsions. Without proper treatment, it will lead to brain damage.” Diagnosis requires collecting and testing spinal fluid, which can only be carried out in a few places in Bangladesh. Testing samples have usually been sent to neighboring India. Bangladesh’s vaccination campaigns have been able to contain measles for decades, but the mass immunization drive that should have taken place in 2024-25 was missed by the caretaker government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, which ruled until mid-February this year. When the outbreak was declared a month later, the new government began emergency measles-rubella immunization in early April and vaccinated 20 million children, but this was not enough to contain the outbreak. Another vaccination drive started on Saturday, targeting 3.4 million children who might have been missed earlier. In case of measles, a highly contagious, airborne disease which is especially dangerous to the under-fives, transmission stops only when immunity reaches 95 percent. “It’s evident that a vaccination failure led us to this measles outbreak. I am not blaming anyone, but there was a gap,” said Mahmuduzzaman. “At the moment, it’s hard to determine how much damage has been done due to this vaccination gap. But due to this outbreak, many children face long-term neurological complications that could leave a portion of a generation disabled.” According to Dr. Ariful Bashar from Infectious Diseases Hospital Mohakhali in Dhaka, SSPE “is estimated to occur in about 1 in every 1,000 cases.” A much more common post-measles condition is immune amnesia, which causes the immune system to forget how to fight off illnesses it has defeated in the past. Children who contract the disease will face its consequences for some years. “Cases of other contagious diseases, especially childhood tuberculosis, are likely to increase ... Infections of the ear and nose, and other respiratory infections also become more likely,” said Bashar. “Measles consequences can be severe as immunity gets suppressed. It may trigger various secondary infections. These suppressed immunity conditions last for a certain period, usually three to four years, or slightly longer.” Follow Topics:measlesBangladesh Related Bangladesh launches measles vaccination drive amid deadly outbreak Bangladesh measles crisis kills more than 1,000 children

content: BOWLING GREEN, Ohio — The Wood County Health Department confirmed one measles case in Bowling Green, Ohio, this week, but warned there was exposure in multiple locations. The individual was infectious during these days and times where they visited: - Bowling Green State University on Sept. 23 in the Overman and/or Physical Science Buildings between the hours of 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. - Pagliai’s Restaurant on Sept. 23 between the hours of 5 p.m. – 9 p.m. - Wood County Hospital Emergency Department on Sept. 24 between the hours of 8:30 p.m. to 1:30 a.m. on Sept. 25 - Wood County Hospital Emergency Department on Sept. 25 between the hours of 6:30 a.m. to 2:15 p.m. - Falcon Health Center on Sept. 28 between the hours of 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Anyone who was in these areas during these times and isn’t properly protected from the virus may have been exposed to measles, the health department warned. For those who haven’t received the MMR vaccine, the health department recommends calling a healthcare provider and to watch for symptoms over the next 21 days. So far in 2026, there have been 196 confirmed measles cases in the state, according to the Ohio Department of Health. The state had 45 cases in 2025, seven cases in 2024, and one case in 2023. Nationally, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 3,659 cases so far this year, already surpassing the number of infections for the entire year of 2025. Measles, which is extremely contagious, is spread through sneezing and coughing. The virus can live up to two hours in the air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. Once breathed in, an individual can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Symptoms include: - Rash - High fever - Running nose - Cough - Loss of appetite - Red, watery eyes The CDC recommends that all children get two doses of the MMR vaccine — the first dose at 12 through 15 months of age, and the second dose at 4 through 6 years of age. Adults who are unvaccinated or don’t know if they received the vaccine can also get one. CDC data shows that vaccination rates for the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Ohio are below the benchmark of the recommended 95% by health officials, as they say 95% vaccination rates in a community can help develop herd immunity to a disease

Pennsylvania reported a fifth death related to measles amid an ongoing outbreak. Callista Images/Image Source/Getty Images The Pennsylvania Department of Health reported a fifth measles-associated death on Wednesday amid an ongoing outbreak that is on track to become the largest the US has seen in decades and has sparked political clashes. The state health department said the person who died was unvaccinated and a resident of Lancaster County, where about 40% of the state’s measles cases have been concentrated. As of Wednesday, Pennsylvania has reported 943 total cases since the outbreak began in April, including at least 176 hospitalizations. All but four of the cases have been among people who were not fully vaccinated. Ad Feedback The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has demonstrated the vaccine’s safety, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. The Pennsylvania health department said that it “will not release any additional details that could personally identify” the person who died. But the department says that the death “meets the measles-associated death definition” and has been reported to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The four other measles-associated deaths reported by Pennsylvania include an unvaccinated teen who lived in Mifflin County, a 40-year old woman in Jefferson County and two infants in Lancaster County. However, the recent deaths have led to a war of words over how measles deaths are counted. The CDC only counts two measles death on its dashboard, but notes that “this number is subject to change; CDC will update its reporting as additional information becomes available and relevant reviews are completed.” Earlier this month, the Pennsylvania health department said that it requested assistance from the CDC’s Epi-Aid program — but Dr. Debra Bogen, department secretary, noted in a letter to CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz that the request would be rescinded “if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths.” However, the US Department of Health and Human Services said that the CDC has not received a formal Epi-Aid request from Pennsylvania. “If requested, CDC stands ready to deploy epidemiologists to support the state’s identified needs,” HHS press secretary Emily Hilliard told CNN in a statement. “Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection.” Pennsylvania Department of Health Press Secretary Neil Ruhland told CNN that “conversations between PA DOH and CDC are ongoing regarding our request for an Epi-Aid.” It has been decades since the United States has tallied this number of measles deaths; 1991 was the last time there were more than four measles deaths in one year. Last year, there were three US deaths from measles – two in Texas and one in New Mexico. Related article CNN Tracking measles cases in the United States 3 min read Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, the Lancaster County coroner, told CNN he’s concerned the outbreak will get worse as the seasons change. Related video Getty Images ER physician: I will perform ‘more spinal taps’ under new childhood vaccine schedule 2:16 “Measles generally, as well as many other respiratory illnesses, does tend to get worse over the fall and winter months,” said Diamantoni, who is also a family physician who says he’s a strong advocate for immunization. “So it very well could become much worse.” Nearly 3,700 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far in 2026, according to data published by the CDC. There haven’t been this many measles cases in the US in any other year since 1991 – surpassing a grim milestone that was just topped last year. Death from measles occurs in one to three patients out of every 1,000 cases, which suggests that the Pennsylvania outbreak may be significantly larger than officially reported case counts suggest. Read Full Bio Dan Raby September 30, 2026 / 2:15 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Georgia health officials have confirmed five measles cases connected to one Jasper County family. With these additional cases, 2026 has the highest number of cases reported in Georgia in the last decade with 21. There were 18 cases reported in 2019. The new cases are siblings who were either unvaccinated or under-vaccinated with at least one sibling having a recent history of out-of-state travel, the Georgia Department of Public Health said in a press release. The Department of Public Health is working to identify anyone who may have been exposed to the virus through contact with the five individuals. These cases are not connected with a recent outbreak linked to a Cobb County day care, the first case of which was confirmed on Aug. 18. The number of cases involved in that outbreak increased to 10 in mid-September. As of Sept. 25, 3,659 cases of measles have been reported across the U.S., the majority of which were in patients 19 years old or younger, data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reveals. That number is nearly 1,400 more cases than all of 2025. Three people have died of measles in Pennsylvania. What are the symptoms of measles? Measles first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes, and a rash. The rash generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and then spreading downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. When the rash appears, the fever may spike over 104 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the CDC. The virus is highly contagious, spreads through the air, and can stay on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has been in a room. Officials have urged residents to get vaccinated, saying that more than 95% of people who receive a single dose of MMR vaccine will develop immunity to the viruses. If you become sick or believe you have been exposed to measles, speak with your healthcare provider immediately but do not go to the doctor's office without first letting them know about your symptoms. You can also call the Georgia Department of Public Health's Acute Disease Epidemiology Section at 404-657-2588 during business hours, Monday through Friday, or 1-866-782-4584 after hours on evenings and weekends. DPH is working to identify individuals who may have been exposed to measles through contact with these individuals. These cases are not related to the earlier outbreak in Cobb County. Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. The measles virus can stay in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has left the room. Measles is highly contagious, but the MMR vaccine can prevent it. Measles symptoms typically appear 7 to 14 days after exposure to the virus, but can be up to 21 days. Symptoms include high fever, cough, runny nose, and watery eyes. Then, a rash of tiny red spots appears starting at the head and spreading to the rest of the body. The MMR vaccine is safe and effective at preventing measles, mumps, and rubella. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that children receive their first dose of the MMR vaccine between 12 and 15 months of age and a second dose between 4 and 6 years of age. For babies aged 6-11 months traveling internationally, the CDC recommends a single dose of the MMR vaccine before travel, followed by two additional doses after their first birthday. Parents with questions about the vaccine or the vaccination schedule should consult their physician. More than 95% of people who receive a single dose of MMR will develop immunity to all three viruses. A second dose boosts immunity, typically enhancing protection to 98%. People vaccinated with the MMR vaccine also help protect others who are too young or medically unable to be vaccinated. Anyone with measles symptoms should contact their healthcare provider immediately. DO NOT go to the doctor's office, the hospital, or a public health clinic without first calling to let them know about your symptoms. Healthcare providers who suspect measles in a patient should notify public health immediately. With these five additional cases, Georgia has 21 confirmed measles cases so far in 2026. Georgia had 10 confirmed measles cases in 2025. Photograph: Hannah Beier/Reuters CDC reports second measles death in US while excluding Pennsylvania deaths Pennsylvania has reported over 900 measles cases and four deaths as governor and health chief RFK Jr spar over data A second measles death in the US has been announced on Tuesday by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), as the country grapples with an outbreak affecting 47 states. As of 24 September, a total of 3,659 measles cases have been confirmed by the CDC, with the two deaths having been confirmed on Tuesday. The confirmation did not specify in which states the deaths had occurred. Although Pennsylvania is the hardest-hit state, having reported more than 900 cases and four deaths from measles, the CDC is not including the deaths there in its national data. Differences in the federal measles death figures compared with those from Pennsylvania’s department of health is part of an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. The CDC, which used to collect data from states, has now shifted to using mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) for its national measles death count. Pennsylvania also reported 114 new cases of measles in the last seven days, with a third of these being children aged under 18. The state has also reported 176 hospitalizations, and less than 1% of the total number of measles cases involve people who have been fully vaccinated against the disease. Pennsylvania’s health department said: “While daily numbers fluctuate, tracking these trends provides Pennsylvanians and health care providers with visibility into community transmission across the [state] and helps inform the department’s ongoing response.” The US has now recorded more measles cases this year than any other since 1991. The disease was declared to be eliminated by the US government in 2000. Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause serious health complications. And although rare, deaths from measles occur in approximately one to three patients per 1,000 cases The announcement also comes as the CDC has faced a dramatic reduction in its work force, with the Trump administration laying off 18% of its staff in 2025. According to the American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE), the largest federal employee union representing 82,000 workers, there are 3,810 fewer civil service employees within the CDC in the past year, a total reduction of a third. Measles symptoms usually begin seven to 14 days after infection, according to the CDC. These symptoms can include high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash that spreads down the body. The CDC advises that two doses of the MMR vaccine “provide the best protection against measles”. content: A microscopic image of the measles virus in cells. CDC Sept. 30, 2026, 7:40 PM UTC / Updated Sept. 30, 2026, 8:34 PM UTC By Jane Weaver Pennsylvania health officials on Wednesday reported the death of an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County who tested positive for measles. It’s the fifth measles-associated death in the state since August. The Pennsylvania Department of Health didn’t report when the individual died. The other measles-associated deaths in the state were two infants with measles in Lancaster County, an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County and a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County. The last two happened in mid-September, state health officials reported. There have been 943 confirmed cases of measles across 39 counties in Pennsylvania, which is dealing with the largest outbreak of the extremely contagious virus in the U.S. About 176 people have been hospitalized. At least six babies have been born with congenital measles in the state. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recognized only two deaths associated with measles this year, although it hasn’t identified in which states they occurred or when. According to the CDC, there have been 3,569 confirmed measles infections nationwide this year. “We are deeply saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania,” Emily Hilliard, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement, adding that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection.”

Measles virus detected in Green Co. wastewater Health officials confirm the detection of measles virus through testing untreated wastewater MONROE — Green County Public Health, in coordination with the Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS), has confirmed a detection of measles virus in untreated wastewater from the City of Monroe in Green County collected on September 16. Wisconsin currently has ongoing measles activity in several other counties throughout the state, with cases identified in Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon counties. As of September 25, there have been 192 measles cases reported in Wisconsin in 2026. To date, no cases have been identified in Green County. When measles is detected in wastewater from a community, it means that one or more people infected with measles were present in the community around the time the sample was collected. Wastewater can represent both the city and the surrounding areas, as well as people who may travel in and out of the area for activities such as work, school, or health care. Someone who does not live in a community could therefore be represented in wastewater while they are there. Green County is working closely with DHS to further investigate the wastewater detection and possible sources. Wastewater monitoring is an important public health tool that has been used in Wisconsin since 2020 to track diseases like COVID-19, and more recently the flu, RSV and mpox. Untreated (influent) sewage from sewage treatment facilities across the state is tested on a regular basis to measure the presence of a given virus in the community. “With measles outbreaks occurring in neighboring communities, testing wastewater for measles is one way we can monitor for disease spread,” said RoAnn Warden, Public Health Officer. “However, wastewater testing alone does not tell us who is sick. This is why it is important for people to ensure that they and their family are vaccinated against measles, are aware of the symptoms of measles, and can talk to their doctor if they are concerned about measles.” Measles is a viral illness that typically begins with a high fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. Within a few days, a rash will appear, beginning as flat red spots on the face, usually at the hairline, and spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. Measles is spread from person to person, often through the air on droplets of saliva. This may look like a sick person coughing or sneezing. The measles virus can stay in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has been in a room and may cause infection in up to 90% of unvaccinated people who are exposed to the virus. Individuals who have the measles can spread the virus to others four days before through four days after the rash appears. If you suspect that you have symptoms of measles, such as a fever, cough, or rash, especially after contact with someone who has measles, please contact a health care provider. Measles can be prevented with the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine (MMR). Two doses of the vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing the disease. In general, people born before 1957 are considered immune and do not need a vaccine. All other adults without laboratory evidence of immunity should have at least one dose of measles-containing vaccine, and children should have two doses. For more information on who should get a measles vaccine, visit the DHS measles webpage. If you do not know if you or your children have been vaccinated to protect against measles, check the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or contact your doctor or local health department. Anyone who may not be vaccinated to protect against measles can still get vaccinated. Your regular health care provider, local clinic or pharmacy, or local health department can help you determine what vaccines you need to protect your health. For free, confidential assistance finding a doctor or clinic near you, dial 211. If you are pregnant, have children under the age of 12 months, or are otherwise not able to receive the MMR vaccine, contact your doctor or community clinic for guidance. See the DHS measles webpage for more information on measles vaccines

content_title: Pennsylvania hits 977 measles cases, while numbers of MMR doses increase
content: WTAJ | Your News Leader Pennsylvania hits 977 measles cases, while numbers of MMR doses increase Cortney Raynor 4 hours ago PENNSYLVANIA (WTAJ) — Measles cases continue to rise as the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH) announced Friday that the outbreak has now grown to 977 confirmed cases across 39 counties, with five confirmed measles-associated deaths. According to the DOH, 34 new positive cases have been reported since Wednesday, with 195 people hospitalized due to the highly contagious respiratory virus. Only four of the cases were among vaccinated individuals, or less than 1% of cases, the agency added. A push for residents to protect themselves and receive the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine has occurred since the outbreak began in April, with pop-up clinics and other community events expanding access to the vaccine. Healthcare professionals across the state have also seen a surge in residents seeking out the MMR vaccine, the DOH notes, with more than 49,000 MMR doses given to residents in August alone — an increase from the 25,000 that are typically given in a month. The figure continues to rise thus far into September, with over 53,000 doses administered. Measles is a serious virus that can cause long-term health problems and can spread when a person who is infected breathes, coughs, or sneezes. The virus can remain in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours, and symptoms typically start between 7 and 21 days after exposure. Lancaster County remains the county with the highest number of measles cases at 383 since April, according to the DOH’s measles dashboard, with local counties like Centre at 21 cases, Jefferson with 44, and Clearfield at 33 cases each. Officials note that the best protection against the measles virus is the vaccine. Residents interested in receiving the required two doses of MMR can contact their health care provider, county or municipal health department, or a Vaccines for Children (VFC) program, to name a few. To learn more about measles and other important information surrounding the virus, visit the PA Department of Health website. Ad Your Privacy Choices

Fresh Air Wild Card with Rachel Martin It's Been a Minute Embedded Get NPR+ More Podcasts & Shows Search Newsletters NPR Shop Get NPR+ Tiny Desk New Music Friday All Songs Considered Music Features Live Sessions About NPR Diversity Support Careers Press Ethics How to protect yourself from measles while traveling Measles is traveling, with outbreaks in Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York, and exposures on transportation and in sports. What should you know before getting on a plane or train? Special Series Living Better Science for a healthy life Travel plans? Here's what to know as measles exposures reach trains and games September 30, 20267:00 AM ET Heard on All Things Considered By Rachel Carlson Measles on the move Listen · 2:25 2:25 Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5978940/nx-s1-9946956" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated. Malte Mueller/Getty Images hide caption toggle caption i Malte Mueller/Getty Images The U.S. is in the midst of the worst measles resurgence in decades. Recent outbreaks in several states and exposures in places like bars, sports stadiums and on public transit have some people questioning the safety of travel or how they should prepare for upcoming plans. Health As diseases loom, CDC's response to measles deaths stirs fears about agency's reliability The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists over 3,600 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of Sept. 24 — and two deaths as of Sept. 28. Almost all of those cases have been among unvaccinated individuals. The CDC notes the number of deaths is subject to change as more information becomes available and after it completes more reviews. It's important to note that the Pennsylvania Department of Health has counted four measles-associated deaths so far. The CDC has disputed whether measles actually caused those deaths. In the last two weeks, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York have had the most cases, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health U.S. measles tracker. The true number of cases across the country is likely higher, according to Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and a professor of pediatrics at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. "I think if anything, we're underestimating how many people are actually being exposed, and how many people are being infected, and how many people are being hospitalized and dying," he said. He said that's because many children, parents or adults may not seek medical care if they get infected. Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter. Dr. Kalyani McCullough, who leads the Vaccine Preventable Disease Epidemiology & Control Section of the Immunizations Branch of the California Department of Public Health, said it's important for people to know that measles is not "just a fever and a rash." "It can affect a lot of different parts of the body, and it can have long-lasting effects as well," she said. "Both with immune amnesia, which means that the measles virus can actually reduce immunity to other infections after being infected with measles." "So I think it's just important for people to realize that getting measles can have some pretty serious consequences," McCullough said. How do you protect against measles? People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles. The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. And you don't have to come in direct contact with someone who has measles to get infected; you just have to be within their airspace within two hours of them being there. Offit said one person with measles can infect about 15 to 18 other people, if they're susceptible. Offit says "susceptible," in this case, means people who've either never had measles, or who are unvaccinated. For people in that category, up to 9 out of every 10 exposed will get measles. What does it mean if there have been measles exposures in my state? Some states that aren't currently experiencing large measles outbreaks have notified residents of possible exposures. While an outbreak is a group of cases in one area during a certain time period, an exposure is when a person comes into contact with someone who has measles, according to George Mason University College of Public Health epidemiologist Amira Roess. Short Wave Vaccinated or not, we're on the brink of a measles epidemic The California Department of Public Health notified people of potential exposures after an infected and unvaccinated train and bus passenger traveled across the U.S. and through multiple California counties. The City of St. Louis Department of Health also encouraged residents to monitor for symptoms after an individual who visited local bars and a sports stadium tested positive for measles. Measles can be difficult for epidemiologists to track because symptoms — like a fever, cough and rash — usually begin seven to 14 days after a person is exposed or as late as 21 days later. Once a person is confirmed to have measles, epidemiologists interview that person and try to figure out the places they visited and people they saw while they were contagious. In the case of measles, that's typically four days before the telltale rash appears and four days after, according to McCullough. Epidemiologists consider that eight-day window the infectious period. "So it's a really labor-intensive process," she said. She said anyone exposed to measles is usually advised to seek medical advice and isolate themselves if they develop symptoms within three weeks of exposure. People who are unvaccinated may be asked to quarantine and may be monitored by public health officials to see if they get sick. What should I do if I'm traveling soon? All the experts who spoke to NPR said the first and most effective step to protect yourself against measles is to make sure you're fully vaccinated. That means having had two doses of the MMR vaccine — commonly done in childhood. You can check with your healthcare provider if you aren't sure about your vaccine status. They may recommend a booster depending on your records and recent health. Offit said this recommendation holds for travelers coming into the U.S. from other countries as well. "I think anybody who is traveling from another country into the United States should make sure they're up to date on their vaccines, because it's dangerous to be in the United States now if you are not fully immune to measles," he said. Offit noted many people who are immunocompromised cannot be vaccinated if they haven't been already. Those people may rely on herd immunity — protection from a disease when a certain percentage of people in a community are vaccinated. For measles, this threshold is 95%. Last school year, kindergarten vaccination coverage dipped to 92.4%, according to the CDC. Children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at around 12 months. But McCullough says if parents are planning to travel internationally with infants or babies 6-11 months old, the CDC's recommendation is to get an early dose of the vaccine. But the experts we spoke to said that if you have your vaccines, you don't need to worry. "If you've been relatively healthy and you are up to date on your vaccines, and you are up to date on your doctor's visits, then you will be fine," Roess said. "I'm not worried about those individuals." Roess also said people can wear masks in busy areas if they are concerned. Clarification: This story has been updated to clarify that measles is infectious for four days prior to and for four days after the onset of a rash. (Getty Images) 0Comment Share topics: Measles Georgia DPH Jasper County MMR vaccine Cobb County daycare Outbreak Unvaccinated Public health JASPER COUNTY, Ga. (WGXA) — The Georgia Department of Public Health (DPH) has confirmed 21 measles cases, with the latest five in Jasper County. In a release, DPH said the five cases were isolated among siblings in a Jasper County family who were either unvaccinated or under-vaccinated. Health officials say only one sibling had a history of out-of-state travel, and they are currently working to determine who may have been exposed to the virus. This comes after the DPH determined that a Cobb County daycare was the center of a measles outbreak at least 10 Metro Atlanta children in the last month. However, officials say these additional five cases are not related. In light of the announcement, Jasper County Charter System said no measles cases were associated with its school district. Powered By 10 NAACP Georgia convention brings branches together in Macon for training and advocacy Share Next Stay "The Jasper County Charter System is aware of recent measles cases confirmed in Jasper County by the Georgia Department of Health. At this time, there have been no measles cases associated with any of our school buildings, and no close contacts have been identified in our schools," the school system said on social media. "We work closely with public health officials. If a student or staff member in one of our schools is ever identified as a case, the district will notify families of that school promptly. We will continue to follow public health guidance and keep families informed if anything changes that affects our schools." DPH says that measles is highly contagious and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and can stay in the air or on surfaces for up to two hours. Symptoms- including a high fever, cough, runny nose, watery eyes and a rash of tiny red spots across the head and body - typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure, or even up to 21 days. READ MORE | Macon woman says insurer denied rehab for chronic pain in new Ossoff report However, health officials say the MMR vaccine can prevent the spread and is safe and effective at preventing measles, mumps and rubella. Anyone with measles should contact their healthcare provider immediately and is urged not to go to the doctor's office, hospital or public health clinic without calling ahead. DPH said Georgia had a total of 10 confirmed measles cases in 2025 and urges anyone seeking information to visit this website or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. content_title: Indiana Warns of Measles Exposure at the Zoo
content: This undated image made available by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows an electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, via AP, File) When an individual infected with measles visited the Fort Wayne Zoo last weekend, Indiana health authorities believe other people at the zoo may have been exposed to the virus. Also known as rubeola, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) describes measles on its website as being a highly contagious viral respiratory illness. The exposure began at the Fort Wayne Zoo on Sept. 27 at approximately 11:30 a.m. and ended at 5 p.m., according to the Allen County Department of Health. The venue is formerly known as the Fort Wayne Children's Zoo and is a popular regional attraction. “As vaccination rates wane and measles continues to circulate in Indiana and across the U.S., exposure to the virus will become more likely,” officials said in a statement online . A total of 24 Measles cases have been reported statewide so far this year, including six in Wayne and six in Switzerland, according to an Indiana Department of Health (IDOH) surveillance tracker. Other cases occurred in Adams, Allen, DeKalb, LaGrange, Ohio, Parke, and Randolph. As of Sept. 26, six of the measles cases required hospitalization. The virus spreads through the air by coughing and sneezing and can linger long after an infected person leaves. As a result, visitors who were at the zoo during the identified time frame are urged to check their measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) immunization record and monitor themselves for symptoms for 21 days. “We are thankful for the Allen County Department of Health for their attentiveness and expertise,” Fort Wayne Zoo executive director and CEO Rick Schuiteman said. “The safety of our guests, staff and volunteers is incredibly important and we will continue to follow the lead of the Allen County Department of Health.” Measles symptoms include a fever of 101 degrees or higher, sore throat, small white spots inside cheeks, red, watery eyes, coughing, runny nose, and a rash that starts on the face and spreads across the body. For those who are unvaccinated and believe they were exposed at the zoo, the health department recommends self-quarantining for three weeks and consulting with physicians. The IDOH surveillance tracker further shows that nine Measles cases occurred in individuals between the ages of 5 and 24 years old, eight cases occurred in individuals between the ages of 25 and 49 years old, and 3 cases occurred among individuals between the ages of 50 and 64 years old. “We urge anyone with questions or concerns to reach out to their local health department or a medical professional,” Schuiteman added. Why did Pennsylvania withdraw its disease regulations? topics: Measles Pennsylvania Outbreak Lancaster Hospitalizations CDC Josh Shapiro Regulations PENNSYLVANIA (WHP) — Pennsylvania measles cases have climbed above 900 as the state has become the center of the outbreak on a national level, accounting for 23.2% of U.S. cases. The Commonwealth has reported 903 total cases of measles, marking a 14% spike from the 792 reported cases based on Sept. 21 data. This surge is consistent with an observed sharp uptick in case totals as we move from summer into fall. Measles cases reported by month in Pennsylvania 2026 (Pennsylvania Measles Dashboard) Hospitalization numbers continue to climb as well, as 21 more Pennsylvanians were admitted to the hospital, bringing the total to 176, according to the Pennsylvania measles dashboard. Additionally, the DOH is reporting four measles-related deaths since the start of 2026. Meanwhile, the CDC is reporting only two measles-associated deaths, which is subject to change as relevant reviews are completed and additional information becomes available. Only two counties have more than 100 reported measles cases, with 363 (40.2%) coming from Lancaster County and 106 (11.8%) cases reported in Mifflin County. Nationally, 61% of cases have been observed in those under the age of 20, with around 1% of reported cases reported in people with unknown ages. Measles cases by age through Sept. 28, 2026 (Pennsylvania Measles Dashboard) In Pennsylvania, more than half of the reported cases have been in residents 24 years and under. According to communications from the Pennsylvania Department of Health (DOH), on Friday, the department withdrew its proposed rulemaking regarding contagious and noncontagious diseases. Pennsylvania House Republicans took to social media, saying the withdrawn "COVID-era" regulatory changes come on the heels of members' concerns about Gov. Josh Shapiro's administrative overreach. The PA GOP said the DOH received more than 6,000 appeals from the public. A West Virginia hospital has identified the first case of measles in the state since 2009, health officials said Monday, April 22, 2024.(Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention via AP, File) By The Associated Press and MIKE STOBBE Published: Sep. 30, 2026 at 11:47 PM UTC Share Add Us On GoogleAdd as a preferred source on Google (AP) - Pennsylvania health officials reported a fifth measles-associated death Wednesday as the U.S. endures its worst year for the disease since 1991. The Pennsylvania Department of Health said the person was from Lancaster County and was unvaccinated. The state did not provide any further information about the person who died. Lancaster County’s coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said that his office did not handle the death and that state officials have not provided him with any details. The state’s other deaths have included an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County, in the center of the state; a 40-year-old woman from Jefferson County, a rural area in western Pennsylvania; and two infants in Lancaster County, in the southeastern part of the state. None of them were vaccinated, according to the state health department. The infants were too young for vaccinations, according to current recommendations. The U.S. has now seen eight reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades. Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak continues to grow, with 943 illnesses reported so far this year across 39 counties. The measles-associated deaths are the first reported in the state in 35 years, state officials say. The nation eliminated the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks. Meanwhile, measles infections have been surging in recent years. In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the U.S. and Mexico have lost their measles-free status. The problem has been years in the making, as fewer kids get routine vaccines because of parental waivers, healthcare access issues and rampant disinformation. More recently, Trump administration health officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have questioned and sown doubt about the established safety of vaccines at an unprecedented level while also defunding local efforts to improve vaccination rates. ___ The Associated Press’ health and science coverage receives financial support from the AP Fund for Journalism and private foundations. content_title: Pennsylvania reports 5th measles-related death in the state
content: Pennsylvania reports 5th measles-related death in the state Updated Wed, September 30, 2026 at 8:34 PM UTC A microscopic image of the measles virus in cells. (CDC) Pennsylvania health officials on Wednesday reported the death of an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County who tested positive for measles. It’s the fifth measles-associated death in the state since August. The Pennsylvania Department of Health didn’t report when the individual died. The other measles-associated deaths in the state were two infants with measles in Lancaster County, an 18-year-old resident of Mifflin County and a 40-year-old woman in Jefferson County. The last two happened in mid-September, state health officials reported. There have been 943 confirmed cases of measles across 39 counties in Pennsylvania, which is dealing with the largest outbreak of the extremely contagious virus in the U.S. About 176 people have been hospitalized. At least six babies have been born with congenital measles in the state. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has recognized only two deaths associated with measles this year, although it hasn’t identified in which states they occurred or when. According to the CDC, there have been 3,569 confirmed measles infections nationwide this year. “We are deeply saddened to hear of another death in Pennsylvania,” Emily Hilliard, spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement, adding that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and CDC Director Erica Schwartz “continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com

content_title: 儿童危及生命麻疹相关心肺衰竭的体外膜氧合(ECMO)救治:病例系列、共感染与抗真菌预防 - 生物通
content: 儿童危及生命麻疹相关心肺衰竭的体外膜氧合(ECMO)救治:病例系列、共感染与抗真菌预防 《European Journal of Pediatrics》:Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for life-threatening measles in children: a case series 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年10月02日 来源:European Journal of Pediatrics 2.9 为了促进科学的传播,生物通采集了这篇文章 订阅BioHot点这里解锁原文链接推送! “畅读会员”点此登录查看原文链接 RESEARCH Open access 麻疹(measles)在全球复燃,尽管疫苗可预防,重症仍可进展为常规支持难以纠正的心肺衰竭。本研究旨在确定体外膜氧合(extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, ECMO)在麻疹患儿中是否可行。研究人员在拥有区域ECMO项目的三级儿科重症监护病房(pediatric intensive care unit, PICU)开展回顾性病例系列,纳入2025年8月至2026年5月暴发期间所有年龄<18岁、实验室确诊麻疹并接受ECMO的儿童。PICU收治49例麻疹患儿,其中10例接受ECMO。5例为男性;中位年龄11个月(IQR,10–24;IQR为四分位距),均未完成适龄疫苗接种。指征为感染性休克或心肺衰竭(n=5)、急性呼吸窘迫综合征(acute respiratory distress syndrome, ARDS)合并感染性休克(n=2)、低氧性呼吸衰竭(n=2)和疑似心肌炎(n=1)。7例接受静脉-动脉(venoarterial, VA)、1例接受静脉-静脉-动脉(veno-venoarterial, VVA)、2例接受静脉-静脉(venovenous, VV)ECMO。5例在ECMO前有菌血症,8例痰培养阳性。前5例患者中3例发生热带念珠菌(Candida tropicalis)念珠菌血症,而在置管时给予抗真菌预防后的后续5例中无一例发生。9例接受评估者中7例存在左心室功能障碍,4例需要减压,8例接受神经影像者中4例异常。6例(60%)存活至出院。结论:ECMO在麻疹相关心肺衰竭中可行且可能挽救生命,生存与其他高急症儿科指征相当,但病程因细菌和真菌共感染、心功能障碍和神经损伤而复杂化。这些资源密集型表现仅发生于未接种疫苗儿童且可预防,强调麻疹疫苗接种覆盖为公共卫生优先事项。已知:麻疹在全球复燃,可在儿童中引起严重呼吸、心脏和免疫并发症。麻疹诱导的免疫抑制易导致继发细菌和真菌感染。新发现:首次报告麻疹ECMO系列:可行,60%生存,但以共感染、心功能障碍和神经损伤为特征。ECMO置管时抗真菌预防与本队列中念珠菌血症消除相关。 研究背景:麻疹(measles)是人类最具传染性的病原体之一,基本再生数估计为12至18。尽管安全有效疫苗已使用半个多世纪,麻疹仍是全球儿童死亡的重要原因。经历数十年下降后,麻疹复燃。COVID-19大流行后,免疫覆盖停滞,随后疾病陡升;2023年全球估计1030万例、超过107000例死亡,多数为5岁以下儿童。接近消除的高收入地区亦未幸免;2025年美国记录30余年来最高病例数,多发生在接种不足社区。此复燃反映大流行期间及之后扩大的疫苗接种缺口,最大暴发集中在覆盖降至群体免疫阈值以下的地区。耶路撒冷地区反复暴发,集中于疫苗接种覆盖欠佳社区,住院儿童并发症负担重。呼吸并发症是幼儿麻疹死亡首位,且因麻疹诱导的免疫抑制而加重。麻疹病毒(measles virus)感染并耗竭记忆淋巴细胞,消除大量既存保护性抗体,并损害B细胞库重建达数月至数年,从而易继发细菌和真菌感染。除肺炎外,重症麻疹可并发喉气管支气管炎、急性脑炎和心肌受累,婴儿及接种不足环境中病死率陡升。多数住院儿童经支持治疗恢复,但一部分进展为危重病,少数发生呼吸或循环衰竭,常规支持耗竭。在少数儿童中,麻疹促发心肺衰竭、重症ARDS、儿茶酚胺难治性感染性休克或心肌功能障碍,常规重症监护无法维持。ECMO是儿童难治性呼吸和心脏衰竭的既定救援治疗,其在小儿呼吸和心脏指征中的应用已扩大。然而,体外支持在麻疹中的可行性、并发症和生存尚未被描述,临床医生在麻疹患儿尽管最大常规治疗仍恶化时缺乏指导。据研究人员所知,尚无系列描述此背景下的ECMO。2025—2026年耶路撒冷大型麻疹暴发期间,空前数量的儿童因麻疹相关心肺衰竭需要ECMO。研究人员描述其临床特征、并发症和结局,以帮助识别和管理危重麻疹患儿,并强调该病的可预防性。研究人员还描述了一项实践改变:在早期观察到真菌共感染后,于置管时引入抗真菌预防。 Agilent Seahorse XF 技术 - 了解功能强大的实时活细胞能量代谢分析系统 领 取 研究人员开展的研究:在Hadassah University Medical Center这一拥有区域PICU和ECMO项目的三级儿科转诊中心开展回顾性病例系列,纳入2025年8月至2026年5月麻疹暴发期间所有年龄<18岁、实验室确诊麻疹并接受ECMO的儿童。麻疹经实时逆转录聚合酶链反应(real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction, real-time RT-PCR)和/或麻疹特异性IgM检测确认。研究遵循流行病学观察性研究报告强化指南(Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology, STROBE),经机构审查委员会批准并豁免知情同意。研究人员从电子病历提取人口学、临床、实验室、微生物、超声心动图、神经影像和结局数据。ECMO按机构和体外生命支持组织(Extracorporeal Life Support Organization, ELSO)方案实施,用于儿茶酚胺难治性心肺衰竭或常规管理无效的难治性低氧性呼吸衰竭。插管模式依据临床选择。抗凝采用普通肝素,插管前50 units/kg弹丸,继以20 units/kg/hour起始输注,调整至抗Xa活性0.2–0.4 IU/mL,并以活化部分凝血活酶时间50–70 s双重监测。所有患儿接受连续超声心动图,神经影像由治疗团队决定。置管后调整通气至肺保护目标,随自体心功能恢复撤减血管活性支持。早期患者发现热带念珠菌(Candida tropicalis)念珠菌血症后,对所有后续患者在插管时引入经验性抗真菌预防。主要关键技术方法可概括为:单中心回顾性病例系列,样本队列来源为2025年8月至2026年5月耶路撒冷麻疹暴发期间PICU收治的实验室确诊麻疹儿童,共49例,其中10例接受ECMO;以real-time RT-PCR和/或麻疹特异性IgM确诊;从电子病历提取多维资料;ECMO按机构和ELSO方案管理,抗凝以普通肝素目标抗Xa 0.2–0.4 IU/mL、活化部分凝血活酶时间50–70 s;统计采用描述性分析,连续变量以中位数(IQR)表示,分类变量以数量(百分比)表示,使用Python 3.12.3分析。上述方法不超过250字。 研究结果:患者特征方面,暴发期间786名儿童在儿科急诊接受麻疹评估,83.4%至少住院1天,49名收入PICU,其中10名接受ECMO并构成研究队列。5名为男性;中位年龄11个月(IQR,10–24),中位体重9.2 kg(IQR,8.0–11.5);10名中7名小于15个月;均未完成适龄麻疹疫苗接种。所有10名接受全身性皮质类固醇,9名接受吸入一氧化氮。疾病严重程度和实验室发现方面,ECMO指征为感染性休克或心肺衰竭5名、ARDS合并感染性休克2名、低氧性呼吸衰竭2名、疑似心肌炎1名;7名存在感染性休克成分。插管时患儿危重,存在严重代谢和呼吸紊乱:中位pH 7.15(IQR,7.06–7.20);乳酸38.7 mg/dL(4.3 mmol/L)(IQR,20.7–63.1 mg/dL;2.3–7.0 mmol/L);氧合指数(oxygenation index, OI)28(IQR,24–29);血管活性-正性肌力评分(vasoactive-inotropic score, VIS)35(IQR,17–52),且均需高浓度氧和血管活性支持。血液学反映麻疹免疫抑制:中位白细胞计数2.4 × 103/μL(IQR,1.0–3.3),8名白细胞减少,1名白细胞增多;中位血小板计数184 × 103/μL(IQR,56–270)。炎症和肝标志物升高:中位C反应蛋白12.0 mg/dL(120 mg/L)(IQR,8.5–14.7 mg/dL;85–147 mg/L);中位天冬氨酸氨基转移酶240 U/L(IQR,180–355);凝血病常见:中位国际标准化比值1.50(IQR,1.11–1.73),中位纤维蛋白原205 mg/dL(2.05 g/L)(IQR,130–342 mg/dL;1.3–3.42 g/L)。尽管中位吸入氧分数100%,气体交换仍严重受损:中位二氧化碳分压52 mm Hg,氧分压57 mm Hg,碳酸氢盐19.3 mEq/L。9名可行超声心动图者中,7名存在左心室或双心室功能障碍,5名为重度。ECMO支持方面,7名接受VA、1名接受VVA、2名接受VV ECMO;1例VA由外周颈部转为中央插管。中位ECMO持续时间10.5天(IQR,6.0–14.2;范围2–60)。VA配置占优反映休克和心功能障碍为主要指征。微生物学方面,ECMO前菌血症5名:肺炎链球菌2名、不可分型流感嗜血杆菌2名、A组链球菌1名。ECMO前痰培养阳性8名:金黄色葡萄球菌7名、A组链球菌2名、肺炎克雷伯菌1名。ECMO期间3名发生念珠菌血症,均为热带念珠菌,且均在前5名治疗患者中;分离株全基因组测序排除共同来源暴发。在插管时引入抗真菌预防后,后续5名均未发生念珠菌血症。并发症和结局方面,重度左心室功能障碍使4名需要左心减压(球囊房间隔造口术3名,外科左房排气1名),其中1名存活。8名接受神经影像,4名异常,分别为硬膜下血肿、多发性脑梗死、深部灰质扩散受限、全脑水肿伴脑疝各1名;这4名中1名存活。全部10名发生急性肾损伤,9名经ECMO回路行血液滤过;7名肝酶异常;3名发生有临床意义的出血。其中2名因此修改抗凝:1名发生黏膜出血后停用肝素,另1名合并黏膜和肺出血者完全暂缓肝素。6名(60%)存活至出院。中位PICU住院时间32.5天(IQR,20.2–51.2;范围3–75),死亡者较短(16.5天,IQR,9.8–31.0),存活者较长(39.5天,IQR,32.2–51.2),与最严重表现早期死亡一致。结局随指征变化:因低氧性呼吸衰竭支持2名均存活;7名有感染性休克指征者中4名存活;疑似心肌炎儿童死亡。死亡与存活儿童比较中,死亡者出血率明显更高(3/4 vs 0/6)。 讨论部分总结:在单次麻疹暴发中,10名儿童,多数为婴儿,因麻疹相关心肺衰竭需要ECMO,6名(60%)存活至出院。据研究人员所知,这是首个报告的麻疹ECMO系列。该队列以严重细菌和真菌共感染、频繁左心室功能障碍需减压以及显著神经损伤为特征,将这些重症监护发现置于麻疹预防失败的更广泛背景中。微生物学谱反映麻疹后深度免疫抑制,耗竭记忆淋巴细胞和既存抗体达数月至数年。半数患者插管前有菌血症,多数呼吸道培养阳性,与此前耶路撒冷暴发中住院儿童并发症谱一致。分离出的肺炎球菌、流感嗜血杆菌、A组链球菌和金黄色葡萄球菌是典型麻疹后细菌重叠感染病原,凸显短暂免疫麻痹造成的脆弱性。更突出的是前5名中3名发生热带念珠菌念珠菌血症;全基因组测序排除共同来源暴发,提示宿主易感性而非院内传播。尽管前后观察不能确立疗效,但在麻疹诱导免疫麻痹背景下,插管时引入抗真菌预防后后续5名无念珠菌血症具有生物学合理性,值得前瞻性评价。侵袭性念珠菌病是免疫受损和体外支持儿童公认且常致命的并发症,热带念珠菌为毒力较强的非白念珠菌种;其仅聚集于最早未预防患者,符合麻疹诱导最大免疫麻痹窗口。期间,对因麻疹需要ECMO儿童保持低阈值抗真菌覆盖似较审慎。心脏受累突出,研究人员经验中作为重症麻疹特征被低估。多数儿童存在重度左心室或双心室功能障碍,4名需左心减压。心肌功能障碍可能反映脓毒症相关心肌病和直接病毒性心肌炎,后者是麻疹罕见但已识别的并发症;尽管ECMO支持心肌炎儿童报告生存约61%,本系列中唯一因疑似心肌炎支持者死亡。左心室扩张是VA ECMO固有风险,逆行动脉血流增加衰竭心室后负荷,除非左心减压,否则可促发肺水肿和出血。观察到的高减压率及这些儿童较差生存支持早期超声心动图监测并低阈值排气。神经损伤频繁且预后差;8名影像儿童中4名异常,从硬膜下血肿和脑梗死到全脑水肿伴脑疝,仅1名存活。此率远高于ELSO登记中儿童ECMO急性神经并发症背景频率,可能反映麻疹相关脑炎、难治性休克缺氧缺血损伤以及体外支持出血和血栓风险汇聚,回顾性队列无法区分,尤其抗凝ECMO期间腰椎穿刺很少可行。麻疹本身引起从急性感染后脑炎到罕见后期亚急性硬化性全脑炎的中枢神经系统疾病谱,观察到的急性损伤可能将这种内在神经嗜性与危重病和体外支持的循环、血液学应激叠加。这些发现的预后权重主张对该人群系统神经监测和神经影像。肾和肝受累近乎普遍:全部10名符合急性肾损伤标准,9名经ECMO回路血液滤过,7名肝酶异常。3名发生出血,均死亡,其中2名相应修改或暂缓抗凝,此模式与出血为最严重病程标志或contributor而非ECMO常规并发症一致。死亡儿童PICU住院短于存活者,反映最严重表现早期死亡而非更长病程。尽管严重,60%儿童存活,与儿科脓毒症和感染性休克ECMO报告结局一致,后者汇总生存接近60%,也与跨儿科ECMO指征累积登记生存一致。麻疹虽未在ECMO指征中单独分类,当常规管理失败时应视为合理指征。值得注意的是,2名因原发性低氧性呼吸衰竭支持者均存活,与儿科呼吸ECMO更有利结局一致;而感染性休克、需减压的左心室功能障碍和神经损伤组合识别出较高风险表型。总体60%生存与当代儿科ECMO跨指征经验一致,表明麻疹本身并不预示徒劳病程。最重要的是,这些发现带明确公共卫生信息。本系列每名儿童均因疫苗可预防感染发生危及生命、资源密集疾病,多数为太小而无法常规接种的婴儿,依赖社区免疫保护。维持至少95%疫苗接种覆盖是阻断传播并保护最年幼群体所需,世界卫生组织推荐对所有急性麻疹儿童辅助维生素A,可降低2岁以下儿童死亡率,该年龄组构成本队列多数。麻疹诱导的免疫遗忘进一步侵蚀人群对无关病原的保护,放大每次暴发的下游发病率,且许多社区覆盖已降至消除阈值以下,包括近期耶路撒冷暴发聚集的接种不足人群。这些措施均不能替代及时2剂免疫提供的一级预防。因小于首剂接种年龄的婴儿尚不能直接保护,其安全依赖阻断社区传播;母体免疫和及时、高儿童期覆盖是关闭该窗口的互补策略。这些病例的资源强度、延长ECMO、多学科重症监护及共感染和神经损伤管理,对面临麻疹复燃的卫生系统有直接意义,主张暴发期间预先规划儿科ECMO能力。前瞻性、多中心合作,包括在国际登记中系统捕获ECMO指征中的麻疹,将有助于界定体外支持在该人群中的作用、最佳时机和结局,并检验抗真菌预防和早期左心减压是否改善生存。在此类数据积累前,研究人员经验支持在经验丰富中心向具有可逆性麻疹相关心肺衰竭儿童提供ECMO,同时认识到最大收益在上游预防。对执业重症医师,即时启示是预见共感染、心脏和神经并发症,早期引入感染病和心脏病专家,并告知家庭基础疾病本可预防。局限:单中心、回顾性病例系列,无对照组;小样本妨碍正式统计推断,ECMO患者选择未方案化。微生物学产量可能低估真实感染负担,抗真菌预防的表观益处来自非对照前后比较,需前瞻性确认。作为描述性系列,不能确立因果关系,单次暴发、单中心设计限制外部效度。研究结论翻译:在本病例系列中,麻疹导致既往健康儿童发生严重到需要ECMO的心肺衰竭,ECMO可行且可能挽救生命。细菌和真菌共感染、左心室功能障碍和神经损伤的负担界定了支持这些儿童的特定挑战。最重要的是,每一例都是疫苗接种覆盖不足所致的可预防后果:麻疹是一种疫苗可预防疾病,保护最年幼儿童依赖通过有效免疫实现的持续高社区免疫。 研究背景:麻疹(measles)是人类最具传染性的病原体之一,基本再生数估计为12至18。尽管安全有效疫苗已使用半个多世纪,麻疹仍是全球儿童死亡的重要原因。经历数十年下降后,麻疹复燃。COVID-19大流行后,免疫覆盖停滞,随后疾病陡升;2023年全球估计1030万例、超过107000例死亡,多数为5岁以下儿童。接近消除的高收入地区亦未幸免;2025年美国记录30余年来最高病例数,多发生在接种不足社区。此复燃反映大流行期间及之后扩大的疫苗接种缺口,最大暴发集中在覆盖降至群体免疫阈值以下的地区。耶路撒冷地区反复暴发,集中于疫苗接种覆盖欠佳社区,住院儿童并发症负担重。呼吸并发症是幼儿麻疹死亡首位,且因麻疹诱导的免疫抑制而加重。麻疹病毒(measles virus)感染并耗竭记忆淋巴细胞,消除大量既存保护性抗体,并损害B细胞库重建达数月至数年,从而易继发细菌和真菌感染。除肺炎外,重症麻疹可并发喉气管支气管炎、急性脑炎和心肌受累,婴儿及接种不足环境中病死率陡升。多数住院儿童经支持治疗恢复,但一部分进展为危重病,少数发生呼吸或循环衰竭,常规支持耗竭。在少数儿童中,麻疹促发心肺衰竭、重症ARDS、儿茶酚胺难治性感染性休克或心肌功能障碍,常规重症监护无法维持。ECMO是儿童难治性呼吸和心脏衰竭的既定救援治疗,其在小儿呼吸和心脏指征中的应用已扩大。然而,体外支持在麻疹中的可行性、并发症和生存尚未被描述,临床医生在麻疹患儿尽管最大常规治疗仍恶化时缺乏指导。据研究人员所知,尚无系列描述此背景下的ECMO。2025—2026年耶路撒冷大型麻疹暴发期间,空前数量的儿童因麻疹相关心肺衰竭需要ECMO。研究人员描述其临床特征、并发症和结局,以帮助识别和管理危重麻疹患儿,并强调该病的可预防性。研究人员还描述了一项实践改变:在早期观察到真菌共感染后,于置管时引入抗真菌预防。研究人员开展的研究:在Hadassah University Medical Center这一拥有区域PICU和ECMO项目的三级儿科转诊中心开展回顾性病例系列,纳入2025年8月至2026年5月麻疹暴发期间所有年龄<18岁、实验室确诊麻疹并接受ECMO的儿童。麻疹经实时逆转录聚合酶链反应(real-time reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction, real-time RT-PCR)和/或麻疹特异性IgM检测确认。研究遵循流行病学观察性研究报告强化指南(Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology, STROBE),经机构审查委员会批准并豁免知情同意。研究人员从电子病历提取人口学、临床、实验室、微生物、超声心动图、神经影像和结局数据。ECMO按机构和体外生命支持组织(Extracorporeal Life Support Organization, ELSO)方案实施,用于儿茶酚胺难治性心肺衰竭或常规管理无效的难治性低氧性呼吸衰竭。插管模式依据临床选择。抗凝采用普通肝素,插管前50 units/kg弹丸,继以20 units/kg/hour起始输注,调整至抗Xa活性0.2–0.4 IU/mL,并以活化部分凝血活酶时间50–70 s双重监测。所有患儿接受连续超声心动图,神经影像由治疗团队决定。置管后调整通气至肺保护目标,随自体心功能恢复撤减血管活性支持。早期患者发现热带念珠菌(Candida tropicalis)念珠菌血症后,对所有后续患者在插管时引入经验性抗真菌预防。主要关键技术方法可概括为:单中心回顾性病例系列,样本队列来源为2025年8月至2026年5月耶路撒冷麻疹暴发期间PICU收治的实验室确诊麻疹儿童,共49例,其中10例接受ECMO;以real-time RT-PCR和/或麻疹特异性IgM确诊;从电子病历提取多维资料;ECMO按机构和ELSO方案管理,抗凝以普通肝素目标抗Xa 0.2–0.4 IU/mL、活化部分凝血活酶时间50–70 s;统计采用描述性分析,连续变量以中位数(IQR)表示,分类变量以数量(百分比)表示,使用Python 3.12.3分析。上述方法不超过250字。研究结果:患者特征方面,暴发期间786名儿童在儿科急诊接受麻疹评估,83.4%至少住院1天,49名收入PICU,其中10名接受ECMO并构成研究队列。5名为男性;中位年龄11个月(IQR,10–24),中位体重9.2 kg(IQR,8.0–11.5);10名中7名小于15个月;均未完成适龄麻疹疫苗接种。所有10名接受全身性皮质类固醇,9名接受吸入一氧化氮。疾病严重程度和实验室发现方面,ECMO指征为感染性休克或心肺衰竭5名、ARDS合并感染性休克2名、低氧性呼吸衰竭2名、疑似心肌炎1名;7名存在感染性休克成分。插管时患儿危重,存在严重代谢和呼吸紊乱:中位pH 7.15(IQR,7.06–7.20);乳酸38.7 vs 0/6)。讨论部分总结:在单次麻疹暴发中,10名儿童,多数为婴儿,因麻疹相关心肺衰竭需要ECMO,6名(60%)存活至出院。据研究人员所知,这是首个报告的麻疹ECMO系列。该队列以严重细菌和真菌共感染、频繁左心室功能障碍需减压以及显著神经损伤为特征,将这些重症监护发现置于麻疹预防失败的更广泛背景中。微生物学谱反映麻疹后深度免疫抑制,耗竭记忆淋巴细胞和既存抗体达数月至数年。半数患者插管前有菌血症,多数呼吸道培养阳性,与此前耶路撒冷暴发中住院儿童并发症谱一致。分离出的肺炎球菌、流感嗜血杆菌、A组链球菌和金黄色葡萄球菌是典型麻疹后细菌重叠感染病原,凸显短暂免疫麻痹造成的脆弱性。更突出的是前5名中3名发生热带念珠菌念珠菌血症;全基因组测序排除共同来源暴发,提示宿主易感性而非院内传播。尽管前后观察不能确立疗效,但在麻疹诱导免疫麻痹背景下,插管时引入抗真菌预防后后续5名无念珠菌血症具有生物学合理性,值得前瞻性评价。侵袭性念珠菌病是免疫受损和体外支持儿童公认且常致命的并发症,热带念珠菌为毒力较强的非白念珠菌种;其仅聚集于最早未预防患者,符合麻疹诱导最大免疫麻痹窗口。期间,对因麻疹需要ECMO儿童保持低阈值抗真菌覆盖似较审慎。心脏受累突出,研究人员经验中作为重症麻疹特征被低估。多数儿童存在重度左心室或双心室功能障碍,4名需左心减压。心肌功能障碍可能反映脓毒症相关心肌病和直接病毒性心肌炎,后者是麻疹罕见但已识别的并发症;尽管ECMO支持心肌炎儿童报告生存约61%,本系列中唯一因疑似心肌炎支持者死亡。左心室扩张是VA ECMO固有风险,逆行动脉血流增加衰竭心室后负荷,除非左心减压,否则可促发肺水肿和出血。观察到的高减压率及这些儿童较差生存支持早期超声心动图监测并低阈值排气。神经损伤频繁且预后差;8名影像儿童中4名异常,从硬膜下血肿和脑梗死到全脑水肿伴脑疝,仅1名存活。此率远高于ELSO登记中儿童ECMO急性神经并发症背景频率,可能反映麻疹相关脑炎、难治性休克缺氧缺血损伤以及体外支持出血和血栓风险汇聚,回顾性队列无法区分,尤其抗凝ECMO期间腰椎穿刺很少可行。麻疹本身引起从急性感染后脑炎到罕见后期亚急性硬化性全脑炎的中枢神经系统疾病谱,观察到的急性损伤可能将这种内在神经嗜性与危重病和体外支持的循环、血液学应激叠加。这些发现的预后权重主张对该人群系统神经监测和神经影像。肾和肝受累近乎普遍:全部10名符合急性肾损伤标准,9名经ECMO回路血液滤过,7名肝酶异常。3名发生出血,均死亡,其中2名相应修改或暂缓抗凝,此模式与出血为最严重病程标志或contributor而非ECMO常规并发症一致。死亡儿童PICU住院短于存活者,反映最严重表现早期死亡而非更长病程。尽管严重,60%儿童存活,与儿科脓毒症和感染性休克ECMO报告结局一致,后者汇总生存接近60%,也与跨儿科ECMO指征累积登记生存一致。麻疹虽未在ECMO指征中单独分类,当常规管理失败时应视为合理指征。值得注意的是,2名因原发性低氧性呼吸衰竭支持者均存活,与儿科呼吸ECMO更有利结局一致;而感染性休克、需减压的左心室功能障碍和神经损伤组合识别出较高风险表型。总体60%生存与当代儿科ECMO跨指征经验一致,表明麻疹本身并不预示徒劳病程。最重要的是,这些发现带明确公共卫生信息。本系列每名儿童均因疫苗可预防感染发生危及生命、资源密集疾病,多数为太小而无法常规接种的婴儿,依赖社区免疫保护。维持至少95%疫苗接种覆盖是阻断传播并保护最年幼群体所需,世界卫生组织推荐对所有急性麻疹儿童辅助维生素A,可降低2岁以下儿童死亡率,该年龄组构成本队列多数。麻疹诱导的免疫遗忘进一步侵蚀人群对无关病原的保护,放大每次暴发的下游发病率,且许多社区覆盖已降至消除阈值以下,包括近期耶路撒冷暴发聚集的接种不足人群。这些措施均不能替代及时2剂免疫提供的一级预防。因小于首剂接种年龄的婴儿尚不能直接保护,其安全依赖阻断社区传播;母体免疫和及时、高儿童期覆盖是关闭该窗口的互补策略。这些病例的资源强度、延长ECMO、多学科重症监护及共感染和神经损伤管理,对面临麻疹复燃的卫生系统有直接意义,主张暴发期间预先规划儿科ECMO能力。前瞻性、多中心合作,包括在国际登记中系统捕获ECMO指征中的麻疹,将有助于界定体外支持在该人群中的作用、最佳时机和结局,并检验抗真菌预防和早期左心减压是否改善生存。在此类数据积累前,研究人员经验支持在经验丰富中心向具有可逆性麻疹相关心肺衰竭儿童提供ECMO,同时认识到最大收益在上游预防。对执业重症医师,即时启示是预见共感染、心脏和神经并发症,早期引入感染病和心脏病专家,并告知家庭基础疾病本可预防。局限:单中心、回顾性病例系列,无对照组;小样本妨碍正式统计推断,ECMO患者选择未方案化。微生物学产量可能低估真实感染负担,抗真菌预防的表观益处来自非对照前后比较,需前瞻性确认。作为描述性系列,不能确立因果关系,单次暴发、单中心设计限制外部效度。研究结论翻译:在本病例系列中,麻疹导致既往健康儿童发生严重到需要ECMO的心肺衰竭,ECMO可行且可能挽救生命。细菌和真菌共感染、左心室功能障碍和神经损伤的负担界定了支持这些儿童的特定挑战。最重要的是,每一例都是疫苗接种覆盖不足所致的可预防后果:麻疹是一种疫苗可预防疾病,保护最年幼儿童依赖通过有效免疫实现的持续高社区免疫。
